desc:
You have the integers of the array nums and may add up to k brand-new integers of your choice to the collection (a new integer may be any value, negative or very large, but adding a value that already exists gains nothing). Afterwards, look for the longest list of consecutive integers x, x+1, ..., x+L-1 all of which are present in the collection. Return the largest L you can achieve.

For example, nums = [1, 2, 4, 7] and k = 2 give 5: add 3 and 5 to obtain the run 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. With k = 0 the question becomes the plain longest consecutive run; with an empty array the answer is simply k.
hints: Repeats are irrelevant: work with the sorted list of distinct values v.
If you choose to cover the stretch from v[i] to v[j], the number of gaps you must fill is (v[j] - v[i] + 1) - (j - i + 1). That must be at most k.

Slide a window [i, j] over the distinct sorted values: shrink from the left while the needed fills exceed k. Any insertions you do not need can extend the run beyond the window, so the answer is the largest window size plus k.
editorial: Let v be the sorted distinct values. A final run covers some stretch of integers; the original values inside it form a contiguous block v[i..j] of the sorted list, and every integer between v[i] and v[j] that is not in the array costs one insertion: exactly v[j] - v[i] + 1 - (j - i + 1) of them.

Windows that fit within the budget k can be found with two pointers, because the cost never decreases when the window grows. For the best window of size w, the remaining budget can always be spent on integers just outside the window, extending the run, so the length is w + k. If the array is empty the answer is k. Time is O(n log n) for the sort and O(n) for the scan.
